a_profitable_day_trading_strategy_for_th.why_promising: Finding: ORB works far better when limited to stocks with unusually high volume, usually because of company news. Heavy relative volume marks the stocks where that imbalance is largest. What would kill it: institutions allowed to trade pre-market, or a fast-moving price discovery process at the open. Decay risk: published 2024 and sits on the retail ORB bandwagon, so check the post-2023 half. Angle for us: the single-stock data is missing, but the 'abnormal volume at the open' filter can be tested as a conditioning variable on ES opening-range breakouts (first-30-minute volume vs a 20-day average) as a proxy for 'index in play'.

an_empirical_evaluation_of_accounting_in.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Accounting Income Numbers
an_empirical_evaluation_of_accounting_in.note: transcript 01 - PEAD (likely not on SSRN; may need the PDF dropped in papers/inbox)
an_empirical_evaluation_of_accounting_in.venue: Journal of Accounting Research, Vol. 6, No. 2 (Autumn 1968), pp. 159-178
an_empirical_evaluation_of_accounting_in.skipped_reason:
Ball & Brown (1968) is the first paper behind post-earnings drift. It has no trading rules, so it gives no tradable edge we don't already have. Breaking it down:
(1) The main finding, a 12-month run-up before the earnings report, is a hindsight artefact. Firms are sorted by a surprise that is only known after the report, and the authors read the run-up as efficient pricing, not as an opportunity. Nothing tells you when to trade before the report.
(2) The only tradable part is the small drift after the report, about 1-2 months. The paper itself measures it at roughly +0.3% for good news and -1.0% for bad news, which is inside the ~1% transaction costs the authors cite. Our existing pead_long strategy already covers this drift: long only, small and mid caps, a 60-day hold, and a positive surprise plus a positive price reaction. pead_next_announcement covers the related repeat-surprise effect.
(3) This paper's one new ingredient is a cruder surprise measure: earnings change versus last year (the 'naive' model). That is a variant or baseline test inside pead_long ("does a consensus-based surprise add anything over the naive year-over-year surprise?"), not a separate strategy.
(4) The index-futures angle (an earnings-season regime filter for ES/NQ) has no support in the paper and no clear WHY at index level. Under our playbook it is a curiosity, not an edge.
(5) Our data can't test it anyway: no single stocks, earnings dates, EPS or consensus estimates.
Recommendation: add the naive year-over-year surprise as a baseline variant to pead_long, and cite this paper as its 1968 source (the price-reaction leg).

analyst_forecast_revisions_and_market_pr.title: Analyst Forecast Revisions and Market Price Formation
analyst_forecast_revisions_and_market_pr.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://ssrn.com/abstract=303980 -> look for 'Download This Paper' (access not confirmed; if it is not free, the Accounting Review version is paywalled and the authors' university pages may host a copy).
analyst_forecast_revisions_and_market_pr.what_it_should_contain: Drift after individual analyst forecast revisions, split by analyst type: herding versus new information, celebrity versus obscure analysts, and wider versus narrower coverage. Revision-based portfolios with abnormal returns over 1-12 months. Needs I/B/E/S analyst estimate data, which we do not have.
analyst_forecast_revisions_and_market_pr.why_promising: Finding: prices adjust only partly to analyst revisions. The delayed reaction is bigger for revisions that carry new information (not herding), for obscure but accurate analysts, and for firms with thin analyst coverage. WHY (slow information diffusion plus attention): the market over-weights celebrity analysts and low-coverage names digest news slowly. This matches the Conti PEAD logic about low analyst coverage, so the edge should live in small/mid caps and in Europe. What would kill it: broader coverage, faster algorithmic parsing of revisions (the paper is from 2003). A good base for rules such as buying after downward-herded or low-coverage upward revisions and holding N days.
analyst_forecast_revisions_and_market_pr.note: Covers the 'analyst recommendation and estimate revision drift' focus area. An alternative with a large body of follow-up work is Barber, Lehavy, McNichols and Trueman, 'Can Investors Profit from the Prophets?' (SSRN 137400).

analyzing_the_analysts_when_do_recommend.title: Analyzing the Analysts: When Do Recommendations Add Value?
analyzing_the_analysts_when_do_recommend.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page (abstract_id=291241), click 'Download This Paper'.
analyzing_the_analysts_when_do_recommend.what_it_should_contain: Portfolio sorts of stocks by consensus recommendation level and by quarterly change in consensus recommendation, run alongside quantitative characteristics (value, momentum, volume). It needs analyst recommendation data (I/B/E/S) and stock prices, neither in our inventory.
analyzing_the_analysts_when_do_recommend.why_promising: Finding: analysts tend to recommend glamour stocks, so the level of the consensus is only useful when it agrees with value and momentum. The quarterly change in consensus is a robust predictor of returns that is orthogonal to many other signals. WHY: slow information diffusion plus analyst incentives. Revisions carry new information that is digested gradually, and the level is contaminated by analyst incentives. That fits the brief's analyst-revision focus and is the better rule frame than buying upgrades blindly. A sister paper, Barber-Lehavy-McNichols-Trueman 'Can Investors Profit from the Prophets?' (SSRN 137400), shows large gross returns to consensus recommendations. A CFA Institute digest of it says the strategy loses its edge after transaction costs. Use that as a warning on turnover. What would kill it: widespread use of recommendation-change screens, or regulation that reduces analyst information advantage (Reg FD).
analyzing_the_analysts_when_do_recommend.note: Chosen over the Barber et al. 'Prophets' paper because the change-in-consensus signal is lower turnover and has a cleaner WHY. Check both for cost drag.

assessing_the_profitability_of_timely_op.title: Assessing the Profitability of Timely Opening Range Breakout on Index Futures Markets
assessing_the_profitability_of_timely_op.where_to_get_it: IEEE Access is open access: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8641124/ -> click 'PDF'. DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2899177. Alternate PDF copies: the scispace link above, or the ResearchGate copy (CC BY-NC-ND).
assessing_the_profitability_of_timely_op.what_it_should_contain: One-minute data on DJIA, S&P 500, NASDAQ, HSI and TAIEX index futures, 2003-2013. Timely ORB (TORB): align the strategy's 'active hours' with when the underlying stock market is open, use a short opening probing window, and trade breakouts. Reports annual returns above 8% in all five markets (p-values below 3%), best probing time per market (short in the US, longer in Asia), and a TAIEX transaction-level check that TORB signals are in the same direction as institutional (especially foreign) traders.
assessing_the_profitability_of_timely_op.why_promising: The only index-futures-specific ORB paper found, and it carries a structural WHY that fits the Conti method: the opening/closing minutes of the underlying cash market carry peak volume and volatility, and breakout signals line up with institutional order flow. We can replicate the idea on ES (1-min, 2013-2026) and test long-only vs both sides, volatility-scaled stops and time exits. Caveats: sample ends in 2013 (alpha-decay risk, check 2014+ out-of-sample), costs and slippage assumptions need checking, and the profits are strongest in Asian markets. A companion working paper by Holmberg, Lonnbark and Lundstrom (Finance Research Letters; crude oil futures only, profits concentrated in 2000-2011) is a cautionary read; a 2026 arXiv paper on MNQ ('Structural Limits of OHLCV-Based Intraday Momentum Signals in MNQ Futures', arXiv 2605.04004) tests ORB and gap signals and reports falsification results, useful as a sceptical benchmark.

closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.title: Closing the Question on the Continuation of Turn-of-the-Month Effects: Evidence from the S&P 500 Index Futures Contract
closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta working paper (via FRASER / FedInPrint)
closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.where_to_get_it: FedInPrint record https://www.fedinprint.org/item/fedawp/13394/original has an 'Access Documents' link to the free full text on FRASER: https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/working-papers-federal-reserve-bank-atlanta-8586/closing-question-continuation-turn-month-effects-656698 . Authors and year are not shown in the search result; check the PDF cover page (it is a 1990s-era Atlanta Fed working paper).
closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.what_it_should_contain: Daily S&P 500 futures returns on the last trading day of the month plus the next three days versus other days. It should show that the effect is strong before 1990 and disappears afterward in both futures and spot, and it argues the disappearance is linked to the shift of individuals from direct stock holding to mutual funds, with turn-of-month patterns being time-varying and microstructure-related. Data: daily futures prices only. Pre-1990 data is not in our inventory, but the 2013-2026 test period can be checked directly with our ES data.
closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.why_promising: FINDING (historical): the turn-of-the-month premium in S&P futures was strong in the 1980s and faded after 1990. WHY: predictable month-end flows (payroll, pension and mutual fund cash reinvestment, institutional liquidity needs), which change with market structure. This is the month-end/quarter-end flow focus area, but note that the paper documents decay, which is useful as a base rate. Later evidence points the other way: Quantpedia cites a statement that the effect is the only persistent calendar effect in S&P 500 futures (Dzhabarov & Ziemba, Journal of Portfolio Management 2010, paywalled), and a 2026 ScienceDirect paper on infrequent rebalancing says the effect persisted in the U.S. through the final five years of its sample. An ES test on 2013-2026 (last day to day +3, or a wider -3/+3 window) would settle which view holds today. Cost of the test is low (long-only, calendar-based, time-exit). Also check it against beta (a long-only calendar strategy in a rising market).
closing_the_question_on_the_continuation.note: Background/decay evidence only. Companion papers to chase if this is useful: Dzhabarov & Ziemba, 'Do Seasonal Anomalies Still Work?' (JPM 36(3), 2010, paywalled, DOI 10.3905/jpm.2010.36.3.093) and 'Infrequent rebalancing, risk deferral, and equity returns at the turn of the month' (ScienceDirect S1042443126000259, 2026). The 'Dash for Cash' paper is already on the known list.

decoding_inside_information.title: Decoding Inside Information
decoding_inside_information.venue: Journal of Finance (NBER Working Paper w16454; SSRN 1692517)
decoding_inside_information.note: Covers the insider-buying focus area. It separates the informative trades from the noise, so it is a rule-writing paper, not just an anomaly paper. One practitioner replication write-up (Equibles, 2026 blog) reports it could not reproduce the routine vs opportunistic split on its own data. Treat as a point to check.
decoding_inside_information.what_it_should_contain: Classification of insiders as 'routine' (same calendar-month trades year after year) or 'opportunistic'. Calendar-time portfolios, 1989-2007: opportunistic trades earned about 82 bp/month value-weighted abnormal return and routine trades roughly zero. Fama-MacBeth regressions on the number of opportunistic buys/sells in a firm-month. Evidence that opportunistic trades predict later news at the firm. Data: Thomson Reuters insider filings (Form 4), CRSP.
decoding_inside_information.where_to_get_it: Free NBER PDF (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w16454/w16454.pdf) or SSRN abstract 1692517 with 'Download This Paper'.
decoding_inside_information.why_promising: Finding: almost all the predictive power of insider trades sits in the irregular, 'opportunistic' trades, mostly purchases. WHY (slow information diffusion): insiders know about upcoming news, they must report with a lag, and the market under-weights a signal that is hidden among routine trades. What would kill it: more attention on Form 4 filings (already automated screens), or insiders shifting to less visible trading. Decay risk: published 2012 and since widely replicated in commercial insider-trading screens; a robustness check by independent users gave mixed results. Angle: long-only, small and mid caps, cluster of buys by several insiders, hold 20-60 days with a time exit. Needs single stocks and insider filing data, so 'no' on our data.

do_s_p500_options_increase_market_volati.title: Do S&P500 Options Increase Market Volatility? Evidence from 0DTEs
do_s_p500_options_increase_market_volati.venue: SSRN working paper (Oct 17, 2025; subsumes the 'Adams, Fontaine, Ornthanalai' 0DTE paper and 'Dim, Eraker, Vilkov: 0DTEs: Trading, Gamma Risk and Volatility Propagation')
do_s_p500_options_increase_market_volati.where_to_get_it: Free PDF from author site: https://www.jean-sebastienfontaine.com/papers/0dte-options-volatility.pdf . Also SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5641974 -> 'Download This Paper'.
do_s_p500_options_increase_market_volati.what_it_should_contain: Intraday evidence that on days with expiring 0DTE contracts, 10-minute realized S&P 500 volatility is lower; that market makers' net gamma (built from option data) predicts lower volatility over the next ~10 minutes, fading after about an hour; and that higher net gamma predicts stronger order-flow REVERSAL and weaker momentum in E-mini futures. Needs SPX option volume/open interest to build gamma (we do not have it); the volatility/reversal behaviour on 0DTE-era vs pre-0DTE days can be tested on our ES data (ES ticks 2021-06 to 2023-06, 1-min to 2026-09; NQ ticks 2021-07 onward).
do_s_p500_options_increase_market_volati.why_promising: Complements the gamma-exposure study already in the method notes (video 04, where crossings continued) with an academic counter-view: net-positive dealer gamma makes hedging counter-directional (dealers trade against the move), which damps volatility and produces reversals in ES; negative gamma does the opposite. Structural WHY = execution mechanics of big players (delta-hedging by market makers) plus limited liquidity in the underlying. Tells us the regime switch: reversion when dealers are long gamma, continuation when short. Edge killers: change in dealer positioning (retail 0DTE selling flipping dealer gamma sign), CME/Cboe product changes. Decay risk: very new (2023-2025), so little crowding evidence yet. Related finding worth cross-checking in the same list: Cboe's paper 'gammasqueezes' estimates the maximum impact of dealer gamma on S&P volatility.

does_overnight_return_predict_the_first_.title: Does overnight return predict the first half-hour return for U.S. market indices?
instruments: S&P 500 index ETF / U.S. market indices
does_overnight_return_predict_the_first_.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5807282 -> click 'Download This Paper' (check the button on the page; free SSRN download assumed, not confirmed in search results).
does_overnight_return_predict_the_first_.what_it_should_contain: Regressions and trading strategies of the first half-hour (09:30-10:00 ET) return on the prior overnight (close-to-open) return for U.S. market indices and ETFs. It should include subsample results by volatility regime (GFC, COVID, post-2010s weakening), a comparison with international index ETFs (where the effect is absent), and strategy performance. All of this can be rebuilt from 1-minute ES/NQ data. ES covers 2013-2026 and NQ covers 2021-2026.
does_overnight_return_predict_the_first_.why_promising: FINDING: A high overnight return negatively predicts the first half-hour return (intraday reversal) in U.S. indices. The effect is stronger in high-volatility periods and weakened after the 2010s. WHY: opposing clienteles. Retail buys overnight (pushing up the open) and arbitrageurs/daytime sellers lean against it. This is the overnight-vs-intraday tug of war applied to the first 30 minutes. It speaks directly to the opening range breakout and gap-fade debate: it says when to fade the gap and when not to. What would kill it: retail overnight demand fading or 24h market makers absorbing it. The paper itself notes the effect weakened after the 2010s, so decay is a real risk. Test it out of sample on 2021-2026.
does_overnight_return_predict_the_first_.note: Complements the known 'Overnight Returns of Stock Indexes: Evidence from ETFs and Futures' (which reports the negative first-30-min relation). This is a newer, focused study with regime and clientele evidence. For ES, define overnight as the 16:00 ET close to 09:30 ET open, or use the globex session; test both.

evaporating_liquidity.title: Evaporating Liquidity
evaporating_liquidity.venue: Review of Financial Studies 25(7); NBER WP 17653; SSRN 1988706
evaporating_liquidity.where_to_get_it: Free PDF from NBER: nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w17653/w17653.pdf. Also on SSRN (abstract_id=1988706).
evaporating_liquidity.what_it_should_contain: Short-term reversal portfolio returns (long recent losers, short recent winners) treated as the return to liquidity provision. Regressions of those returns on lagged VIX. Conditional Sharpe ratios by VIX bucket. Industry-portfolio reversal results. Replicating it needs CRSP-style daily stock returns and VIX, neither of which we hold. VIX history is free, but stock data would have to be sourced elsewhere.
evaporating_liquidity.why_promising: Finding: short-term reversal profits are strongly time-varying and highly predictable from the VIX. Conditional Sharpe ratios rise sharply when VIX is high. WHY: liquidity provision, a risk/liquidity premium plus forced selling. When intermediaries are capital-constrained, they pull back, the price concession on forced sellers grows, and whoever steps in is paid more. It fits the brief's fund-flow forced-selling area and sits next to the known 'Asset Fire Sales' paper. It gives a simple volatility-regime rule: fade losers harder when VIX is elevated. What would kill it: abundant, unconstrained liquidity supply (HFT/market makers with ample capital) compressing the premium. Another risk is that reversal alpha is thin after costs, so check the decay over time.
evaporating_liquidity.note: Also a useful bridge to our index-futures work: the same VIX-conditioning idea can be tried on ES/NQ short-term reversal.

from_drift_to_reversal_temporal_changes_.title: From Drift to Reversal: Temporal Changes in Delayed Price Reactions to Earnings Announcements
from_drift_to_reversal_temporal_changes_.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5836584 -> try 'Download This Paper'. SSRN usually offers a free PDF for working papers, but I have not confirmed it. If it is blocked, try the authors' university pages.
from_drift_to_reversal_temporal_changes_.what_it_should_contain: Tests of how this quarter's earnings news predicts the market reaction at the next quarter's earnings announcement. Evidence that the old continuation turned into reversal after about 2002 and appears only for positive news. Splits by aggressive trading at the current announcement and by limits to arbitrage. Needs single-stock returns, SUE/EPS and announcement dates, which we lack.
from_drift_to_reversal_temporal_changes_.why_promising: Finding (as stated in the abstract): the old pattern in which good earnings news kept pushing prices up at the next earnings date has flipped to a reversal since about 2002. A PEAD-style strategy earns negative returns at the following announcement, concentrated in positive news and in high limits-to-arbitrage stocks. WHY: investors who learned PEAD now trade aggressively on it ahead of time, so the next announcement is overpriced. That is crowding, an execution/behavioural reason, which also says when it dies (less crowding). Gives a tradable 'fade the extrapolated winner into the next earnings date' angle. Decay risk is the main point: this is a recent paper, so check whether the reversal is itself being arbitraged away.
from_drift_to_reversal_temporal_changes_.note: Complements Martineau: drift is gone, and at the next announcement it has turned to reversal. Backs the 'earnings-day gap fade' angle in the Stocks track. A very recent working paper, so I have not verified its PDF access.

gamma_fragility.title: Gamma Fragility
gamma_fragility.venue: SSRN working paper (University of St. Gallen / Imperial College)
gamma_fragility.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3725454 -> 'Download This Paper'. A free PDF copy is on the University of St. Gallen repository (see pdf_url). A March 2021 version is at tashfeenomran.com/DB/Research Papers/Gamma Fragility.pdf.
gamma_fragility.what_it_should_contain: Builds a proxy for aggregate dealer gamma imbalance from options data, using a large panel of equity and index options. The sample includes S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq 100 and Russell 2000 plus 276 stocks. Expect regressions of intraday 5-minute return autocorrelation on the sign of ex-ante gamma imbalance, and on the interaction with illiquidity. Also expect tables on the link to flash-crash frequency and size. Needs options open interest or gamma data, which we do not have. We can only test the price-side regime, for example intraday autocorrelation split by volatility or illiquidity proxies, on ES and NQ 1-min bars.
gamma_fragility.why_promising: Finding: intraday momentum shows up when dealers are net short gamma, and reversal when they are net long gamma. The effect is stronger when the underlying is less liquid. WHY (execution mechanics of big players / forced hedgers): option market makers must delta-hedge mechanically. Short-gamma dealers trade with the move and long-gamma dealers trade against it. The edge weakens if dealer positioning becomes less concentrated or if more non-dealer liquidity absorbs the hedging flow. This is the academic root of the gamma-exposure study on our desk (note 04). Useful for deciding when to apply continuation versus reversion rules on ES and NQ. The Baltussen et al. paper on hedging demand is already known, so this adds the intraday autocorrelation side and the stock-level evidence.

intraday_0dte_option_order_flow_and_s_p_.what_it_should_contain: A study of 1,027 trading days (May 2022 to June 2026) of same-day S&P 500 options. The opening put-call ratio, weighted by gamma, is related to the next hour's return and to the chance the hour contains a negative return. Expect an out-of-sample check of a trading rule built on the signal, results before and after costs, and an analysis that separates how often a fall occurs from how deep it is. Needs intraday 0DTE option flow data with quote classification and Greeks, which we do not have, so this is not testable on our data. The price side can only be approximated with ES.
intraday_0dte_option_order_flow_and_s_p_.why_promising: Finding: a put-heavy gamma-weighted opening flow predicts a weaker next-hour return and a higher chance of a negative hour, but the authors report that the out-of-sample trading rule earns no significant return, before or after costs. WHY (dealer hedging, forced gamma hedgers) is the same as in the gamma-exposure study on our desk, but the paper is a useful negative result: information is not the same as a tradable edge. Read it as a reality check before building any 0DTE-flow-based ES rule, and as a guide to what the outcomes look like when the signal fails out-of-sample. Recent (2026), so the decay risk is unknown and the result has not been peer reviewed.

intraday_patterns_in_the_cross_section_o.title: Intraday Patterns in the Cross-section of Stock Returns
intraday_patterns_in_the_cross_section_o.note: Covers the intraday momentum / cross-section / liquidity-forced-trading areas. The authors link the pattern to institutional order splitting. Sits near 'Market Intraday Momentum' (already known) but is a different, single-stock-level pattern. The authors present the result as concentrated in the first and last half hours.
intraday_patterns_in_the_cross_section_o.what_it_should_contain: Cross-sectional regressions of each stock's half-hour return on its own past returns at lags that are exact multiples of one trading day. Result: continuation that lasts about 40 trading days, stronger in the first and last half-hours, and not explained by volume, spreads or the Keim (1989) bid-ask effect. Separate result: short-term reversal is driven by temporary liquidity imbalances lasting under an hour. Stock-level intraday data needed, but the time-of-day structure can be partly tested on ES 1-minute bars (same half-hour of yesterday predicting today's same half-hour) 2013-2026.
intraday_patterns_in_the_cross_section_o.where_to_get_it: Free: arXiv abs/1005.3535 ('View PDF'). Also on SSRN abstract 1107590 ('Download This Paper') and on the University of Houston Bauer site (PDF).
intraday_patterns_in_the_cross_section_o.why_promising: Finding: a stock's return in a given half hour predicts its return in the same half hour on following days, for about two months. WHY (Conti pattern 'liquidity constraints on large orders / execution mechanics'): big funds split a parent order over many days and trade at similar times of day, so flow is persistent and predictable. What would kill it: faster, randomized execution algorithms (VWAP/TWAP with randomization, dark pools), and lower trading costs. Decay risk: published 2010, and algorithmic execution has changed a lot since, so the out-of-sample half matters. Angle: apply to ES/NQ time-of-day returns, plus use it as a timing guide for entries.

It should also include the U-shaped intraday patterns and the log-linear 'invariance' relation between return variance per trade and trade size. intraday_trading_invariance_in_the_e_min.why_promising: Not a directional edge: it is the structural map of ES liquidity and volatility by time of day. WHY it matters: volatility per unit of volume is time-of-day dependent, so range-based sizing (contracts = dollar risk / ATR or range) and noise-band widths should be time-of-day aware, and quiet Globex hours behave differently from the RTH open and close. This supports the volatility-targeting step in Conti's sizing box, and the 'overnight session ORB' angle and the 30-minute noise-barrier work. It can also sanity-check slippage assumptions at the open, lunch and close.

market_return_around_the_clock_a_puzzle.what_it_should_contain: Average E-mini S&P 500 excess return by time of day over a ~24h session, 2006-2018 (plus 2020 COVID check). Main claim: the four hours around the European open account for the entire average return, with a 1.6 Sharpe that stays high after costs and positive returns every year; the other 20 hours are a noisy zero. Also VIX-futures evidence (uncertainty rises overnight, falls at the European open). Needs only ES intraday bars, which we have.
market_return_around_the_clock_a_puzzle.why_promising: Directly extends the 'overnight drift' idea Conti uses but is not in our already-known list. Finding: the overnight premium is concentrated in a ~4-hour window around the European open (roughly 02:00-06:00 ET). Structural WHY (risk/liquidity premium + information accumulated while the US is closed): uncertainty builds during Asian hours and is resolved when European investors process it. That gives a precise clock-time window we can turn into a simple long-only 'European-open' ES rule and a 'different session' angle. What would kill it: 24h participation by US desks / Asian-session price discovery, or the VIX-uncertainty pattern vanishing. Decay risk: published 2020, so check the 2019-2026 out-of-sample portion of our ES data (our ES 1-min covers 2013-2026 in UTC; remember DST handling for European open).

No drift for glamour stocks. Tables by book-to-market quintile. Needs repurchase announcement dates and fundamental data (not held).
market_underreaction_to_open_market_shar.why_promising: Finding: buyback announcements are followed by long-run abnormal returns, and almost all of the effect sits in value stocks, where the repurchase signals undervaluation. WHY (slow information diffusion / underreaction): the market ignores much of the signal in the announcement, and managers buy because of undervaluation, not hype. What would kill it: widespread knowledge, buybacks used for EPS management or option-offsetting (not undervaluation), and later studies finding weaker long-run drift. Decay risk is high (1995). Angle: test only short-horizon drift after the announcement for small/mid-cap value names, or in Europe, where the regulatory regime differs (see Råsbrant on Stockholm, SSRN 1780967, for a European check).
market_underreaction_to_open_market_shar.note: Covers the 'share buyback announcements' focus area. Later studies (Peyer and Vermaelen 2009; Bargeron et al. 2017) find weaker or timing-dependent returns, so treat this as a starting point to read alongside them.

nasdaq_100_index_futures_intraday_moment.title: Nasdaq-100 Index Futures: Intraday Momentum or Reversal?
nasdaq_100_index_futures_intraday_moment.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=712168 -> click 'Download This Paper' (download availability not confirmed in search results; if the button is missing, search the title on Google Scholar).
nasdaq_100_index_futures_intraday_moment.what_it_should_contain: Multiple regressions of today's intraday NQ-futures returns on yesterday's return and last night's return. It conditions on the signs of those returns, bull versus bear markets, and day of week (Monday effects). Expect results by intraday period, including four opening-hour periods where the forecast model works. Last night's return is mainly associated with reversal, while yesterday's return gives both momentum and reversal. The sample is pre-2005, so it is an out-of-time check for us. Our NQ 1-min data starts in 2021-07, so we can re-test the same regressions on 2021-2026 (partial). ES can serve as a longer-history proxy.
nasdaq_100_index_futures_intraday_moment.why_promising: Finding: NQ futures show both momentum and reversal in the opening hours, depending on the sign of the overnight and prior-day returns and on Mondays. The authors point to a structural feature of the futures market in the opening hours. WHY (information while the market is closed, digested on the open): overnight returns reverse after the cash open, while the prior day's return carries over. It is old and the effect size is uncertain, so treat it as a hypothesis generator, not a rule to copy. Its value is the conditioning grid (overnight sign x prior-day sign x weekday), which is cheap to test on NQ and ES, in-sample first. Expect the effect to have decayed since 2005, so a post-2021 test is a real out-of-sample check.

new_evidence_on_stock_price_effects_asso.title: New Evidence on Stock Price Effects Associated with Changes in the S&P 500 Index
new_evidence_on_stock_price_effects_asso.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page (abstract_id=6851), click 'Download This Paper' (free SSRN login may be needed).
new_evidence_on_stock_price_effects_asso.what_it_should_contain: Event-study tables for post-October-1989 S&P 500 changes. Abnormal returns on the announcement day, between announcement and effective date, and after the change, plus volume. It needs single-stock prices and the index change dates (S&P press releases), neither in our inventory.
new_evidence_on_stock_price_effects_asso.why_promising: Finding: after the 1989 rule change, which made additions public in advance, additions earn positive abnormal returns on the announcement day and in the run-up to the effective day. Deletions show the mirror image, and the move is only partly reversed afterwards. WHY: forced, predictable trading by index funds and benchmarked managers. They must buy on the effective date, and arbitrageurs front-run them. That is a calendar-driven execution constraint. It is the natural historical companion to the known 'Disappearing Index Effect' paper (Greenwood-Sammon). That paper shows the effect fell from about 7% in the 1990s to under 1%, so this paper gives the original mechanism and the window structure to test whether any piece survives. What would kill it: crowded front-running, or indexers moving to more flexible or delayed implementation. Greenwood-Sammon finds the announcement effect is now much smaller.
new_evidence_on_stock_price_effects_asso.note: Old paper, high decay risk. Read it for the mechanism and event windows, not as a live edge.

news_driven_return_reversals_liquidity_p.title: News-Driven Return Reversals: Liquidity Provision Ahead of Earnings Announcements
news_driven_return_reversals_liquidity_p.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2275982 -> click 'Download This Paper'. A free author-accepted copy is also on MIT DSpace (the pdf_url above). The journal version is on ScienceDirect (paywalled).
news_driven_return_reversals_liquidity_p.what_it_should_contain: Event-time plots of short-term return reversals around earnings announcements. Calendar-time long/short tests: a 3-day pre-announcement return sort gives 145 bps in the announcement window versus 22 bps in non-announcement periods. Cross-sectional tests on inventory risk and information asymmetry. To replicate we would need single-stock daily/intraday prices plus earnings announcement dates, which we do not have.
news_driven_return_reversals_liquidity_p.why_promising: Finding: losers-before-earnings beat winners-before-earnings by about 145 bps over the announcement window, roughly six times the normal reversal. WHY (liquidity premium plus execution mechanics of big players): market makers hold inventory into a binary news event, so they demand a bigger concession for absorbing order flow in the days before earnings. That concession is paid back when the uncertainty resolves. It maps to the pre-earnings run-up / earnings-day fade focus area. What would kill the edge: market makers hedging event risk cheaply with options or ETFs, or tighter liquidity provision by HFT firms. Decay risk: published 2014, so check post-2014 data. Angle: pair the 3-day pre-earnings loser/winner flag with a one-day or overnight holding period over the earnings gap, and test it on liquid large caps and on small caps.
news_driven_return_reversals_liquidity_p.note: Fills the 'pre-earnings run-up and earnings-day gap continuation / fade' focus area. It supplies a clear structural WHY (market-maker inventory risk) that fits the Conti method. Also related to the known Earnings Announcement Premium papers, but it is a different mechanism.

noise_band_intraday_momentum_in_nasdaq_1.what_it_should_contain: A step-by-step degradation of the Zarattini et al. (2024) noise-area intraday momentum strategy from the published SPY specification to an executable NQ micro-contract version. It should include a lookahead audit of the trailing stop, slippage stress tests (one index point of slippage on stop fills removes about 22% of the edge), a three-year block-bootstrap of drawdown (95th-percentile max drawdown of $3,406 as backtested and $4,081 with lag and slippage), and minimum account size. Data: NQ 1-minute bars (we have NQ from 2021-07 as 1-min).
noise_band_intraday_momentum_in_nasdaq_1.why_promising: FINDING: The ORB-style noise-area momentum edge on SPY partly survives on NQ futures at one micro contract but shrinks materially once realistic fills and lag are applied. WHY: the same overnight-information/opening-imbalance and institutional-mandate logic as the Conti opening range method (the 1987 noise-area paper and Zarattini et al. are already on our known list). The value of this paper is not a new anomaly but a ready-made validation recipe: lookahead audit, execution stress, block-bootstrap drawdown and sizing. It tells us how much of a published edge to expect after costs, exactly the 'don't copy the paper' lesson. It also tests a different instrument (NQ), which is Conti's 'find the angle'. Decay risk: very recent, so check its out-of-sample period against our 2021-2026 NQ data.
noise_band_intraday_momentum_in_nasdaq_1.note: Very new (about a week old in search results); a single-author or practitioner-style working paper, so treat claims with caution and verify in our own backtest. Useful for the validation stage rather than as a source of an independent WHY.

order_consolidation_price_efficiency_and.title: Order Consolidation, Price Efficiency, and Extreme Liquidity Shocks (S&P 500 futures quarterly expiration / witching days)
order_consolidation_price_efficiency_and.venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis (author names from memory of the paper, not shown in the search snippet; confirm on the PDF title page)
order_consolidation_price_efficiency_and.where_to_get_it: Free PDF from Terrence Hendershott's Berkeley Haas page: https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/hender/Witching.pdf (direct download). Also findable on SSRN by title.
order_consolidation_price_efficiency_and.what_it_should_contain: An event study of quarterly S&P 500 futures expiration ('triple witching') days. Because S&P 500 futures and options settle on the opening prices of the index stocks, arbitrage unwinding creates large order imbalances at the open. Expect tables of opening imbalances, price impact and reversal after the open on NYSE versus Nasdaq stocks, and how fast prices rebound. Our ES data (ETH/RTH 1-min since 2013, ticks 2021-06 to 2023-06) can test the price path from the Thursday close through the 9:30 ET open and the first hour on expiry Fridays. The stock-level order imbalance data is not available to us.
order_consolidation_price_efficiency_and.why_promising: Finding: expiration-day settlement at the open creates large, largely informationless order imbalances. The paper's own sample was built to study liquidity shocks, and a related literature reports predictable index moves on these days. WHY (forced trading / execution mechanics): index arbitrageurs and hedgers must unwind or settle at a known time. They trade regardless of price, so the price moves temporarily and then reverts. The edge would shrink if settlement changes, for example away from the opening quotation, or if more liquidity providers target the imbalance (decay risk). Fits next to the known 'Derivative Payoff Bias / Third Friday Price Spike' paper but focuses on the order imbalance and the post-open reversal, which gives an intraday ES rule with a time exit. Also covers futures roll and settlement effects.

The core signal is long assets with a low prior-day overnight return and short assets with a high one. premium_for_heightened_uncertainty_expla.title: Premium for Heightened Uncertainty: Explaining Pre-Announcement Market Returns
premium_for_heightened_uncertainty_expla.venue: NBER WP 25817; Journal of Financial Economics 145(3), 2022

It uses S&P 500 index futures to measure returns from the close to just before the release, which is mostly the overnight session. price_drift_before_u_s_macroeconomic_new.title: Price Drift before U.S. Macroeconomic News: Private Information about Public Announcements?
price_drift_before_u_s_macroeconomic_new.venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 54(1):449-479 (ECB Working Paper No. 1901)
price_drift_before_u_s_macroeconomic_new.where_to_get_it: Free ECB working paper PDF: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/scpwps/ecbwp1901.en.pdf . SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2637528 -> 'Download This Paper'. Journal DOI 10.1017/S0022109018000625.
price_drift_before_u_s_macroeconomic_new.what_it_should_contain: Second-by-second E-mini S&P 500 and 10-year Treasury futures around 21-30 U.S. macro announcements (about 2003/2008-2014; versions differ on exact counts). Finds a pre-announcement drift in the 'correct' direction starting roughly 30 minutes before the release, accounting for about 40% (earlier version: half) of the total price adjustment, in only some announcements, with an estimated profit of about USD 20 million a year; explanations tested are leakage and proprietary data; stricter release procedures (e.g. PFEI guidelines) make the drift less likely. Testing the signal needs announcement surprises (consensus vs actual) and release times, which we do not have; a surprise-free version can only test ES volatility and the 30-minute run-up on release days.
price_drift_before_u_s_macroeconomic_new.why_promising: Adds a different WHY to the pre-FOMC drift we already know: informed traders and information leakage/proprietary data collection push futures prices before 08:30 ET releases (NFP, CPI etc.), so the early move can be traded in ES with a short time exit. Edge killers: tighter release security/lock-up procedures (the same authors' later paper 'Drift Begone!' shows drift disappears when procedures change) and faster algos pricing the leak. Decay risk is high: sample ends 2014; companion evidence from Kurov, Wolfe and Gilbert, 'The Disappearing Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift' (SSRN 3134546), shows the pre-FOMC drift essentially vanished after 2015, so this should be read together with it to avoid over-trusting old results. Treat as an event-study design to rebuild on ES 1-min with a hand-built release calendar.

rest_in_peace_post_earnings_announcement.title: Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
instruments: US single stocks (large caps and microcaps)
rest_in_peace_post_earnings_announcement.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3111607 -> click 'Download This Paper' (free, 46 pages; the latest version is Aug 2021). The Critical Finance Review also hosts the published version.
rest_in_peace_post_earnings_announcement.what_it_should_contain: Drift (CAR) tests by year and size bucket. It argues the earnings surprise is fully priced on the announcement day in modern markets. It reports large-cap drift as non-existent since 2006 and microcap drift as gone only recently. It adds recommendations for measuring PEAD correctly (announcement timing, intraday windows). Data needed to replicate: single-stock prices, EPS and consensus estimates, and announcement timestamps, none of which we hold.
rest_in_peace_post_earnings_announcement.why_promising: This is the key decay-risk paper for any PEAD idea. Finding: the post-announcement drift has vanished in large caps (since about 2006) and recently in microcaps, because prices now absorb the surprise on the announcement day. WHY (slow information diffusion / liquidity constraints, now eroded): faster, cheaper trading removed the delayed reaction. The surviving angle is therefore the announcement-day / first-day gap itself, not multi-week drift. It must be read before any PEAD rules are written, because it tells us what would kill the edge and where to look for what is left (small/mid caps, Europe, where coverage and liquidity are lower). Note the contrary evidence in the 2025-26 literature (Hirshleifer, Peng and Wang; Dickerson, Julliard and Mueller) as cited in a Subrahmanyam SSRN note.
rest_in_peace_post_earnings_announcement.note: Counterpoint to the known 'A Review of the PEAD' and 'Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?'. It stops us copying 1989-style PEAD rules that no longer work.

reversal_momentum_and_intraday_returns.title: Reversal, Momentum and Intraday Returns
reversal_momentum_and_intraday_returns.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page (abstract_id=2991183), click 'Download This Paper'. A PDF mirror is also in the pdf_url field, but SSRN is the primary source.
reversal_momentum_and_intraday_returns.what_it_should_contain: Stock-level momentum strategies on the first 2 hours (about 9:30-11:30) of returns and reversal strategies on the last 2 hours. Fama-MacBeth regressions, 5-factor alphas (about 0.50% monthly for the afternoon reversal after controlling for conventional reversal), and robustness to standard momentum and reversal factors. Full replication needs intraday single-stock data. We can only run the index-level analogue (first and last 30-120 min of ES/NQ), which is related to the known 'Market Intraday Momentum' paper.
reversal_momentum_and_intraday_returns.why_promising: Finding: morning returns positively predict future returns (continuation) and afternoon returns negatively predict them (reversal), at the single-stock level. WHY: information versus liquidity. The first hours carry information-driven trades, since news arrived overnight and is being digested. Late-day trades are liquidity-driven (rebalancing, forced flows) and later revert. This is the 'closed market, slow digestion' and 'forced flows' pattern in one paper. It also gives a stock-level version of gap-and-go intraday continuation and an afternoon fade. What would kill it: faster price discovery, as the open absorbs overnight news, or late-day liquidity provision becoming more competitive. Treat it as unproven, since it is a working paper and a single author with little follow-up in the results I found.
reversal_momentum_and_intraday_returns.note: Working paper; the author's sample and period should be checked in the PDF. Partial testability only via ES/NQ first/last-hours proxy.

short_interest_returns_and_fundamentals.title: Short Interest, Returns, and Fundamentals
short_interest_returns_and_fundamentals.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page (abstract_id=2216919), click 'Download This Paper'. The 2017 Financial Management version is paywalled.
short_interest_returns_and_fundamentals.what_it_should_contain: Monthly short-interest decile sorts, regressions of short interest on future earnings surprises, news and analyst forecast revisions, and splits by how hard stocks are to short. Replication needs bi-monthly short interest (FINRA/Exchanges), CRSP, I/B/E/S and Compustat, none of which we hold.
short_interest_returns_and_fundamentals.why_promising: Finding: high short interest predicts bad news, negative earnings surprises and downward analyst revisions several months ahead. The usual short-interest/return relation vanishes once those fundamentals are controlled for. WHY: informed trading, plus short-sale frictions that slow the pass-through. Short sellers act on information early, and the price adjusts slowly, which makes short interest a leading indicator of negative earnings surprises. This links the short-interest, borrow-fee and PEAD focus areas. It suggests an angle: use short interest as a filter to avoid longs ahead of earnings, or to select the short side of post-earnings drift. The known 'Loan Fee Anomaly' paper is the borrow-cost companion. What would kill it: short-interest data becoming widely used in real time (more frequent reporting), or short selling becoming cheaper, which Diamond-Verrecchia argue makes short sales less informative.
short_interest_returns_and_fundamentals.note: Related: Rapach-Ringgenberg-Zhou 'Short Interest and Aggregate Stock Returns' (SSRN 2474930) finds aggregate short interest is the strongest known predictor of market returns. That one could be tested on ES if we obtained monthly short-interest data.

the_52_week_high_and_momentum_investing.why_promising: Stocks near their 52-week high keep outperforming. WHY: traders anchor on the 52-week high and under-react to good news near it. Also tested on index level in later work.
the_52_week_high_and_momentum_investing.what_it_should_contain: Ranking by price / 52-week high, holding periods, comparison with classic momentum.

the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.title: The Derivative Payoff Bias (later retitled "The Third Friday Price Spike"; earlier version "The Equity Derivative Payoff Bias")
the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.venue: SSRN working paper (Revise & Resubmit, Review of Financial Studies)
the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4562800 -> click 'Download This Paper'. Free alternatives: AFA conference copy at https://afajof.org/management/viewp.php?n=98196, or the paper link on Julian Terstegge's site (julianterstegge.com). Use the newest SSRN version (the 'Third Friday Price Spike' revision) if listed. Search results show earlier (Sep 2023) and later versions with different headline numbers (about 10 bps open-to-open vs 14-18 bps), so check which version you have.
the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.what_it_should_contain: Return profile of S&P 500 futures/SPX from the 3rd-Thursday close through the 3rd-Friday 9:30 ET open (the special opening quotation, SOQ) and the reversal by about noon. It should split the effect into quarterly (larger, roughly 26 bps) and off-quarterly expiries. It should also cover the pre-/post-2006 overnight-trading break, the 5-minute VWAP return construction, and the evidence on market-maker 'charm' hedging and manipulation. Data: intraday SPX/ES prices plus an option expiry calendar. It uses only index and futures prices, so it needs no extra data.
the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.why_promising: FINDING: Equity prices drift up from Thursday close to Friday open on monthly option-expiry dates and then fully revert, because most index derivatives settle on the opening print. WHY: derivative settlement design plus intermediary hedging. Option market makers' charm-related delta hedging, or possible manipulation, happens in the illiquid overnight window just before the settlement price is set. This is a clean 'institutional constraint / execution mechanics' WHY. It maps onto the focus areas option expiry, futures roll/settlement and overnight session. It gives a calendar-based, rule-friendly pattern: long ES from Thursday RTH close into Friday 09:30 ET, then flat or fade after the open. What would kill it: moving settlement away from the AM open (the authors propose this), or dealers changing how they hedge. Decay risk: the paper is recent and covered by Bloomberg/Barron's, so it may be getting arbitraged.
the_derivative_payoff_bias_later_retitle.note: Not on the already-known list. It is the only paper found that ties third-Friday/quad-witching settlement mechanics directly to an ES overnight-to-open drift and reversal. Our ES 1-min ETH data (2013-2026, UTC; convert to ET) covers about 150 expiry Fridays, including about 50 quarterly ones, which is thin, so use confidence intervals. Check the roll: on quarterly expiries trade the next contract, not the expiring one.

the_disappearing_index_effect.title: The Disappearing Index Effect
the_disappearing_index_effect.note: Directly relevant to the 'index addition and deletion' focus area. It is also the best worked example of how a forced-flow edge decays and why, which is the main lesson of the playbook's decay-risk step. Not on the known list (Russell Reconstitution Effect is already known, this is different).
the_disappearing_index_effect.what_it_should_contain: S&P 500 addition/deletion abnormal returns from 1980 to 2020, by decade (about 10% in the mid-1990s falling to near zero). Split between 'migrations' from S&P MidCap and direct additions (direct additions about 5.4% vs migrations about -1.8% in the 2010s). Passive-fund net demand, evidence on front-running and shrinking trading costs, and a short section on Russell index changes (weaker, not significant). Data: S&P addition/deletion dates (Siblis), CRSP, fund holdings.
the_disappearing_index_effect.where_to_get_it: Free PDF on the HBS research page (hbs.edu/ris/download.aspx?name=ssrn-4294297.pdf), or the NBER version w30748 (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30748/w30748.pdf), or SSRN abstract 4294297 with 'Download This Paper'.
the_disappearing_index_effect.why_promising: Finding: the S&P 500 inclusion pop has declined sharply and is close to zero on average. The effect survives only where the net demand shock is still large (direct additions, large weights). WHY (Conti pattern 'institutional constraint / mandate' plus 'liquidity constraint on large orders'): index funds must buy on the effective date, but liquidity providers and front-runners now absorb the flow in advance. That tells us exactly what to test: condition on the size of net passive demand. What would kill it: front-running capacity, midcap-fund offsets, and rule changes in S&P announcement timing. Decay risk: already high, and the paper documents it. Use as a template for deciding which forced-flow edges are still alive. Single-stock and event-date data not in our inventory.

the_earnings_announcement_premium_and_tr.title: The Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume
the_earnings_announcement_premium_and_tr.note: Core reference for the pre-earnings run-up and earnings-day buying topic. Other papers in this area (uncertainty resolution, over-extrapolation) build on it. Cited here from the SSRN abstract page.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_and_tr.what_it_should_contain: Stocks rise on average around scheduled earnings dates. Calendar-time portfolio returns for stocks in or out of their predicted announcement month. Volume surges around announcement dates. Link between high past announcement-period volume and the highest premium. Imputed small-investor buying (from trade size). Needs CRSP, earnings dates (Compustat/IBES) and trade-size data.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_and_tr.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page abstract_id=986940, click 'Download This Paper'. The NBER version is Working Paper w13090 on nber.org, usually a free PDF there too.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_and_tr.why_promising: Finding: stocks earn an abnormal return around scheduled earnings dates, strongly tied to volume surges. WHY: attention-driven retail buying. The announcement draws small investors, who are net buyers of attention-grabbing stocks, and the order flow is predictable because the dates are known in advance. That fits the 'someone is predictably forced or likely to trade' test. What would kill it: retail attention shifting away from earnings dates, or arbitrage capital pre-positioning earlier and earlier. Decay risk: published 2007 and widely known (also shown in 46 countries by Barber et al., SSRN 1872183, a good follow-up for the Europe angle). Angle: long-only, buy about 5-10 days before the known earnings date and exit before or at the print, avoiding the surprise risk. Needs earnings dates and single-stock prices, which we do not have.

the_earnings_announcement_premium_around.title: The Earnings Announcement Premium Around the Globe
the_earnings_announcement_premium_around.where_to_get_it: Free PDF from co-author Reuven Lehavy's Michigan page (webuser.bus.umich.edu/rlehavy/BDLT.pdf). Or the SSRN abstract page (abstract_id=1872183), click 'Download This Paper'.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_around.what_it_should_contain: About 200,000 annual-earnings announcements from 46 non-US countries over 20 years. Average return in announcement months vs non-announcement months, year-by-year and country-by-country consistency, and a cross-country regression linking the premium to the rise in idiosyncratic volatility around announcements. To replicate it you need single-stock prices and earnings calendars, which we don't have. A first pass could use ES/NQ returns during peak earnings-season weeks.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_around.why_promising: Finding: stocks earn about 11% a year more in earnings-announcement months than in other months, and this holds outside the US. It covers the 'Europe' angle in the brief. WHY: a risk/uncertainty premium. Holders are paid for carrying uncertainty about the coming earnings news, and the premium is largest where idiosyncratic volatility jumps most at announcements. That is the same pattern as the overnight drift, a payment for carrying risk. What would kill it: regulatory disclosure that removes the uncertainty before announcements. The companion paper 'The Disappearing Earnings Announcement Premium' (Heitz et al., SSRN 3296537) finds the premium vanished after 2004 disclosure rules. Read it alongside this one to check decay. Also see Gao, Hu & Zhang, 'Uncertainty Risk Resolution Before Earnings Announcements' (SSRN 3595953), which finds 72% of the premium arrives before the release. That points to a tradable pre-earnings run-up window of about 10 days.
the_earnings_announcement_premium_around.note: Covers the pre-earnings run-up and Europe/international focus areas. Not in the already-known list (the known one is Frazzini-Lamont's 'Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume').

the_information_content_of_annual_earnin.title: The Information Content of Annual Earnings Announcements
the_information_content_of_annual_earnin.note: Companion paper showing price and volume reactions around the announcement. It also supports the finding that information is concentrated in the announcement month.

the_loan_fee_anomaly_a_short_seller_s_be.title: The Loan Fee Anomaly: A Short Seller's Best Ideas
the_loan_fee_anomaly_a_short_seller_s_be.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3707166 -> 'Download This Paper'. A free PDF copy is also at the pdf_url above.
the_loan_fee_anomaly_a_short_seller_s_be.what_it_should_contain: Comparison of the loan fee predictor with 102 other anomalies (Green-Hand-Zhang set) and other short-selling measures. Long-short monthly returns by loan-fee bin (4.01% headline monthly spread; 0.48% after the GHZ-style adjustment). Persistence over time and the share of loan-fee alpha unexplained by other anomalies (about 42%). Needs stock loan fee data (e.g. Markit/IHS securities lending), which we do not have.
the_loan_fee_anomaly_a_short_seller_s_be.why_promising: Finding: stocks that are expensive to borrow underperform, and loan fee is described as the best single cross-sectional return predictor. WHY (risk premium / short-sale constraint plus informed shorting): short sellers pay high fees only when they have strong convictions, so high fees reveal informed bearish bets, and the constraint stops the price correcting immediately. It also shows where other anomalies live (the short leg of expensive-to-borrow names). What would kill it: cheaper, more abundant lending supply, or crowded short trades that squeeze. The practical point for us: the short side of most stock strategies (PEAD, momentum) may be uninvestable after borrow cost. Pair it with Muravyev, Pearson and Pollet, 'Anomalies and Their Short-Sale Costs' (SSRN 4266059), which finds average anomaly returns go to about zero after borrow fees.
the_loan_fee_anomaly_a_short_seller_s_be.note: The known list already has the option-implied borrow fee paper. This is the more direct loan-fee evidence and works as a gate for any short-side idea. It also frames squeeze risk.

the_overnight_drift.title: The Overnight Drift
the_overnight_drift.where_to_get_it: Free NY Fed Staff Report 917 PDF (newyorkfed.org)
the_overnight_drift.why_promising: E-mini returns concentrated around 2-3 a.m. ET (European open), explained by dealers' inventory risk from end-of-day order imbalances. Their July 2026 follow-up (Liberty Street Economics, 'The Disappearing Overnight Drift') says the effect has been near zero since 2021 - a direct test of Conti's overnight claim.
the_overnight_drift.what_it_should_contain: Hour-by-hour E-mini returns 1998-2020, link to closing order imbalance; timing rules for an overnight window

the_pre_fomc_announcement_drift.where_to_get_it: NY Fed Staff Report 512 (free on newyorkfed.org) - search 'Lucca Moench pre-FOMC announcement drift staff report'
the_pre_fomc_announcement_drift.why_promising: S&P 500 rose a large share of its total return in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements. Later work (SSRN 'The Disappearing Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift') says it faded - test both on ES.

the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.title: The Role of Leveraged ETFs and Option Market Imbalances on End-of-Day Price Dynamics (revised as: Liquidity Provision to Leveraged ETFs and Equity Options Rebalancing Flows: Evidence from End-of-Day Stock Prices; JFQA)
the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.venue: SSRN / Swiss Finance Institute working paper; later published in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.where_to_get_it: Free PDF of the Sept 2021 version: https://alexandria.unisg.ch/bitstreams/5a99db31-0d37-4f86-9502-8cb0f3bff4fe/download (University of St. Gallen repository). The revised version is on SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3925725 -> 'Download This Paper'. The published JFQA version is DOI 10.1017/S0022109025000225 (likely paywalled).
the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.what_it_should_contain: Evidence that large negative aggregate option gamma imbalance (scaled by dollar volume) produces end-of-day momentum in the last half hour, and positive gamma produces reversal. It should also cover a separate leveraged-ETF rebalancing effect (formula from Cheng & Madhavan), timing of hedging windows (option dealers hedge about an hour before the close, LETFs only at the close), Sharpe ratios of the strategies, and the finding that LETF effects are shrinking while gamma effects persist. Data it needs: option open interest/gamma by strike and LETF AUM. We lack both, so a pure replication is not possible. An index-level proxy for the LETF rebalancing flow (sign and size of the day's S&P/NDX return times the AUM leverage factor) can be tested on ES/NQ 15:00-16:00 ET returns.
the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.why_promising: FINDING: The last half hour is predictable from the size of forced hedging flow. LETF sponsors and option market makers must rebalance delta in the direction of the day's move when they are short gamma, which creates momentum into the close. When they are long gamma the flow reverses. WHY: execution mechanics and mandated rebalancing, a hard-wired and timed flow (leveraged ETFs must rebalance at the close). This is a structural WHY for last-30-minute drift in ES/NQ. What would kill it: LETF providers spreading their hedges over the day (the paper already shows this shrinking effect), or dealers changing hedge timing. It adds a flow-based rationale and a conditioning variable (large day move times large gamma/LETF AUM) to the known 'Market Intraday Momentum' and 'Hedging Demand and Market Intraday Momentum' papers.
the_role_of_leveraged_etfs_and_option_ma.note: Not on the known list. The two versions have different titles; read the 2021 version first for the cleanest end-of-day story. The sample is mostly single stocks, so treat the ES/NQ extension as our own angle. Test: condition 15:30-16:00 ET (or 15:00-16:00) ES/NQ return on the sign and magnitude of the day's move so far, split by high vs low LETF-proxy size.

the_russell_reconstitution_effect.title: The Russell Reconstitution Effect
the_russell_reconstitution_effect.where_to_get_it: SSRN abstract 278000; follow-up 'Russell Reconstitution Effect Revisited' is SSRN 960727
the_russell_reconstitution_effect.why_promising: Index funds must trade every addition/deletion on reconstitution day, creating order imbalances and price pressure. The 2007 follow-up says the effect has weakened - check what survives.
the_russell_reconstitution_effect.what_it_should_contain: Abnormal returns from rank day to reconstitution day for additions vs deletions; reversal afterwards. Needs Russell membership lists.

the_unintended_consequences_of_rebalanci.title: The Unintended Consequences of Rebalancing
the_unintended_consequences_of_rebalanci.venue: SSRN / NBER Working Paper w33554 (rev. Jan 2026); working paper, forthcoming status not confirmed
the_unintended_consequences_of_rebalanci.where_to_get_it: Free PDF (AFA conference copy): https://afajof.org/management/viewp.php?n=144452 . SSRN abstract page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5122748 -> 'Download This Paper'. NBER version: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w33554/w33554.pdf (may need a subscription).
the_unintended_consequences_of_rebalanci.what_it_should_contain: Sample 1997-2023 using S&P 500 and 10-year Treasury note futures returns. 'Calendar' and 'Threshold' rebalancing signals built from a 60/40 portfolio drifting from target; when stocks are overweight, funds sell equities and buy bonds, and next-day equity returns fall by about 17 bps. Predictability concentrated around month-end, robust to momentum/reversal/macro controls, with Sharpe ratios for a front-running rule and robustness tables (including end-of-month reversal). Needs 10-year note futures/Treasury returns to build the stock-vs-bond signal; ES alone only lets us test the month-end calendar part.
the_unintended_consequences_of_rebalanci.why_promising: Gives a modern, quantified WHY for month-end and quarter-end ES flows that is better than the generic 'turn of the month' story: institutional mandate/constraint (pension funds, target-date funds, balanced funds must rebalance to fixed weights on known schedules), so their trades are mechanical and predictable. Tradable idea: fade or front-run equity weakness after strong stock-vs-bond outperformance into month-end, long-only/short-only variants. Edge killers: funds randomising or smoothing rebalancing, front-runners (some pensions reportedly trade it themselves) crowding the trade. Decay risk: moderate; widely discussed by sell-side desks (month-end pension rebalance estimates) since before this paper. Needs a ZN (10-year note) series, which is not in our inventory, so mark data as partial.

understanding_intraday_momentum_strategi.title: Understanding intraday momentum strategies
understanding_intraday_momentum_strategi.note: Shows predictability weakened after 2013 and depends on volatile regimes. This is directly relevant to decay risk and regime filtering.

understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.title: Understanding Returns to Short Selling Using Option-Implied Stock Borrowing Fees (Is There a Risk Premium in the Stock Lending Market? Evidence from Equity Options)
understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.venue: Working paper (December 2017 draft; AEA 2018 program / UNC)
understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.note: Covers the short-interest and borrow-fee focus area. It is mainly a cost reality check: it argues that the short-interest anomaly is largely a compensation for borrow fees. Listed so the desk does not build a naive 'short heavily-shorted stocks' strategy. The published title/venue may differ from the working-paper title shown here; check the final journal version when downloading.
understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.what_it_should_contain: Portfolio sorts on short interest, lending supply, utilization and borrow fees. Result: returns to short selling net of borrowing costs are less than one-third of the gross returns and not significant. Option-implied borrowing fee (from put-call parity) equals quoted fee on average, and predicts returns at 1-week and 1-month horizons, including in hard-to-borrow stocks. Needs data: stock-lending data (Markit/IHS), OptionMetrics, CRSP.
understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.where_to_get_it: Free PDFs: the UNC finance site (jhfinance.web.unc.edu ... 2017JH_MuravyevPearsonPollet.pdf) or the AEA 2018 conference program page for the 'Understanding Returns to Short Selling Using Option-Implied Stock Borrowing Fees' draft. Search the title on SSRN for the latest version.
understanding_returns_to_short_selling_u.why_promising: Finding: short-interest and borrow-based signals predict poor returns, but after borrow costs most of the edge is gone, and what remains is predicted by option-implied fees. WHY (Conti pattern 'risk premium / constraint'): short sales are limited by lending supply, so overpricing persists only where borrowing is costly or scarce, and borrow fee is the price of that constraint.
